Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

**The value is a finite nonnegative real.** For $n\ge 1$ the norms
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

**At $n=0$ the convention is explicit.** The only element of $\mathbb{R}^{0}$
is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

The induced quantity is a norm on the matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$:
for each rational $p\ge1$, and likewise for the separately named
$\infty$-case when $m,n\ge1$, separation, absolute homogeneity and the triangle
inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

Let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$ and let $m,n,q\in\mathbb{N}$, with the
induced $p$-norms of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

1. **Compatibility.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and every
   $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert Ax\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert x\rVert_p.$$
2. **Submultiplicativity.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and
   $B\in M_{n\times q}(\mathbb{R})$,
   $$\lVert AB\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert B\rVert_p.$$
3. **Normalisation.** For every $n\ge 1$,
   $$\lVert I_n\rVert_p=1,$$
   where $I_n$ is the identity matrix of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]];
   at $n=0$ the unique empty matrix $I_0\in M_0(\mathbb{R})$ has
   $\lVert I_0\rVert_p=0$, the convention of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
For every real $x$, the series $\sum_{n\ge0}x^n/\iota(n!)$ converges absolutely. Its power-series radius is therefore $+\infty$.

Matrix multiplication over a field is associative and unital, distributes over
entrywise addition on both sides, and is compatible with scalar multiplication.
Precisely, whenever the displayed products have compatible shapes,

$$A(BC)=(AB)C,\qquad I_mA=A=AI_n,$$

$$(A+A')B=AB+A'B,\qquad A(B+B')=AB+AB',$$

$$0B=0=A0,\qquad (\lambda A)B=\lambda(AB)=A(\lambda B).$$

These identities include every zero-sized shape.

**Natural exponents, in a monoid.** Let $(M,\cdot,e)$ be a monoid
([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]) and $g \in M$. By the recursion theorem
([[thm-recursion]]), applied with the set $M$, the element $e$ and the function
$x \mapsto x \cdot g$ from $M$ to $M$, there is exactly one function
$\mathbb{N} \to M$, written $n \mapsto g^{n}$, with

$$g^{0} = e, \qquad g^{\sigma(n)} = g^{n} \cdot g \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

In particular $g^{0} = e$ for **every** $g$, including $g = e$, and
$g^{1} = g^{\sigma(0)} = e \cdot g = g$. Since $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$
([[def-natural-numbers]]), the exponent $0$ is a genuine value of the definition
and not a separate convention.

**Integer exponents, in a group.** Let $G$ be a group ([[def-group]]) and
$g \in G$. Write $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ for the embedding
$\iota(k) = [(k,0)]$ of [[lem-nat-embeds-int]], which is injective, preserves
addition, multiplication and order, and has as image exactly the nonnegative
integers. For $x \in \mathbb{Z}$ define

- $g^{x} := g^{k}$, the natural power, when $0 \le x$ and $x = \iota(k)$;
- $g^{x} := (g^{k})^{-1}$ when $x < 0$ and $-x = \iota(k)$.

**Why this is well defined.** The order on $\mathbb{Z}$ is total and
antisymmetric ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]], [[def-int-order]]), so exactly one of
$0 \le x$ and $x < 0$ holds and the two clauses never both apply. In the first
clause $x$ is nonnegative, so $x = \iota(k)$ for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$, and $k$
is unique because $\iota$ is injective. In the second clause $x < 0$ gives
$0 = x + (-x) < 0 + (-x) = -x$ by compatibility of the order with addition
([[thm-int-ordered-ring]], [[def-int-operations]]), so $-x$ is a positive integer
and again $-x = \iota(k)$ for a unique $k$. The inverse $(g^{k})^{-1}$ is a single
determined element by [[lem-inverse-unique]] and [[def-invertible-element]].
Finally the two readings of $g^{\iota(k)}$, as a natural power and as an integer
power, agree by construction, so no ambiguity is introduced.

**Abbreviation.** In an exponent we write $k$ for the integer $\iota(k)$ when a
natural number $k$ is used where an integer is expected; this is unambiguous
because $\iota$ is injective and preserves the arithmetic and the order, and
because the two readings of $g^{k}$ agree as just noted.

**Additive notation.** When the group is written additively the same object is
written $n g$ or $n \cdot g$ rather than $g^{n}$, with $0 g = 0$ and
$\sigma(n) g = n g + g$; the definitions are identical, only the symbols differ.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ with $m\ge 1$ and $n\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$, with the induced $1$-norm and the
separately defined induced $\infty$-norm of
[[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

1. **Maximum column sum.** $\lVert A\rVert_1=\max_{j<n}\sum_{i<m}|a_{ij}|$.
2. **Maximum row sum.** $\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|$.

**The factorial.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to the
set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

**Four facts, proved here because the page uses each of them.**

**(a) The factorial is the product of the first $n$ positive naturals.**
$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]. Induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

**(b) $n! \ne 0$, and $\iota(n!) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{j<n}\iota(j+1)$.** For the
first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ ([[thm-omega-is-peano-system]]) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
([[lem-nat-mult-identity]]) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
([[lem-nat-mult-cancellative]]). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

**(c) $n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$ for $k \le n$.** Induction on $k$, for
all $n$ at once. At $k = 0$ this reads $1 \cdot n! = n!$. Assume it at $k$ and
let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have
$k + d = n$ and $d \ne 0$, since $k + 0 = k \ne n$; so $d = \sigma(e)$ for a
unique $e$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]), and $\sigma(k) + e = n$, that is
$e = n - \sigma(k)$ ([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
([[lem-nat-mult-associative]], [[lem-nat-mult-commutative]]) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

**(d) Boundary values.** $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ for every $n$, by the base
clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional ([[def-nat-multiplication]]), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

derivations.claim: If $A$ has size $0\times0$, the matrix space has one element, which is both $0$ and $I_0$; every partial sum in the definition is this same matrix. Thus $e^{tA}=I_0$ for every $t$, its derivative is the zero matrix, and the derivative identities, initial value, and commuting-product identity all hold because every product and sum is the unique empty matrix. Hence assume below that $A$ has size $n\times n$ with $n\ge1$.

Put $M=\|A\|_1$. By induction using [F1] and [F4], $\|A^k\|_1\le M^k$ for every $k\ge0$. For $|t|\le T$, [F5] then bounds each entry of $t^kA^k/k!$ by $(TM)^k/k!$. The scalar majorant converges by [F2], so each entry series converges absolutely and uniformly on $[-T,T]$; its entrywise sums define a matrix $E(t)$. Each column has only $n$ entries, so the maximum-column-sum formula [F5] bounds the norm of a matrix tail by $n$ times the scalar majorant tail. Therefore the matrix series converges in induced $1$-norm uniformly on $[-T,T]$. Since $T$ was arbitrary, it converges locally uniformly and defines $e^{tA}=E(t)$.

Fix $c\in\mathbb R$ and choose $R>|c|$. If $|h|<R-|c|$, then $|c|,|c+h|<R$; for $k\ge1$, the factorization $(c+h)^k-c^k=h\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(c+h)^{k-1-j}c^j$ bounds the norm of the $k$th matrix-series difference quotient by $M^kR^{k-1}/(k-1)!$, and the same bound holds for the $k$th proposed derivative term $c^{k-1}A^k/(k-1)!$. The sum of these bounds is $M\sum_{j\ge0}(MR)^j/j!<\infty$ by [F2]. For each finite partial sum, the factorization also shows that its difference quotient tends to the finite sum of the proposed derivative terms, using $(k+1)!=(k+1)k!$ from [F6]. For each fixed nonzero $h$, the full difference quotient is the limit of those of the finite partial sums by [step 1.2]; the two uniform tail bounds let us first choose a large partial sum and then take $h\to0$. Consequently $E$ is differentiable at $c$ and $E'(c)=\sum_{k\ge1}c^{k-1}A^k/(k-1)!$.

From [F3] and the recursive power definition [F4], induction gives $A^k=AA^{k-1}=A^{k-1}A$ for every $k\ge1$. Hence the derivative series in step 1.3 is the limit of both $A\sum_{j=0}^{N}c^jA^j/j!$ and $\bigl(\sum_{j=0}^{N}c^jA^j/j!\bigr)A$ as $N\to\infty$. Submultiplicativity [F1] makes multiplication by fixed $A$ continuous, so these limits are $AE(c)$ and $E(c)A$. At $c=0$, all positive-degree terms vanish and the constant term is $A^0=I_n$. Thus $E'(c)=AE(c)=E(c)A$ and $E(0)=I_n$.

Suppose $A,B\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ commute. For each $r\ge0$ set $D_r:=\sum_{m=0}^r A^mB^{r-m}/(m!(r-m)!)$. Induction from $AB=BA$ and [F3] gives $B^sA=AB^s$ for every $s\ge0$. Distributing $D_r(A+B)$ and using this commutation, the coefficient of $A^jB^{r+1-j}$ is $1/(j!(r-j)!)+1/((j-1)!(r+1-j)!)$ for $1\le j\le r$, which equals $(r+1)/(j!(r+1-j)!)$ by [F6]; for $j=0$ and $j=r+1$ the single endpoint coefficient has that same value by $(r+1)!=(r+1)r!$. Thus $D_r(A+B)=(r+1)D_{r+1}$. Since $D_0=I_n$, induction, the recursive power law [F4], and the nonzero factorial images in [F6] give $D_r=(A+B)^r/r!$ for every $r$.

Apply the power bound and convergence argument of step 1.2 to $B$ and $A+B$ as well. Put $a_m=\|A\|_1^m/m!$ and $b_n=\|B\|_1^n/n!$; both scalar series converge by [F2]. The finite product $E_N(A)E_N(B)$ expands by [F3] as the square sum over $0\le m,n\le N$ of $A^mB^n/(m!n!)$, whose term norms are at most $a_mb_n$ by [F1] and [F4]. Its difference from the triangular sum over $m+n\le N$ has norm at most $(\sum_{m>N/2}a_m)(\sum_n b_n)+(\sum_m a_m)(\sum_{n>N/2}b_n)$, which tends to zero; every omitted pair has $m>N/2$ or $n>N/2$. By step 1.2, $E_N(A)E_N(B)\to e^Ae^B$ (matrix multiplication is continuous by [F1]); by step 3.1 the triangular sum is $\sum_{r=0}^N(A+B)^r/r!$, which converges to $e^{A+B}$. Therefore $e^Ae^B=e^{A+B}$.

Step 1.1 covers the zero-sized matrix case. For $n\ge1$, steps 1.2 and 1.3 establish convergence and differentiation, step 2.1 gives the derivative identities and initial value, and steps 3.1–3.2 prove the commuting-product identity. Thus every claim in the Statement holds.

boundaries.evidence: Proof step 1.1 treats a zero-by-zero matrix separately: every partial sum is the unique empty matrix, equal to the empty identity; all derivative and product identities hold there.
Proof step 2.1 sets the scalar argument to zero and obtains the constant power A^0=I. For a zero matrix, step 1.2 has norm bound M=0 and every positive power vanishes, so the series is the identity.
Proof step 1.1 passes to every positive matrix dimension, including one; step 1.2 uses the maximum-column-sum formula, which for a one-entry matrix is its absolute value.
Proof steps 1.2 and 3.1 require only finite matrices and, for the product formula, commutation. No inverse, rank, or nonzero matrix norm is used; the zero-sized branch is discharged in step 1.1.

Proof step 1.3 fixes an arbitrary real differentiation point c and chooses R>|c|, so negative, zero and positive c are covered without a time-domain endpoint restriction. Step 2.1 explicitly gives E(0)=I.

boundaries.reason: Entrywise exponential sums are uniquely defined limits of prescribed partial sums; the real local radius can be chosen explicitly larger than the fixed argument. No selector for a family of nonempty sets is required.
The exponential-series lemma asserts convergence, differentiation, an initial value and a commuting-product identity; it does not characterize any condition by a necessary implication.
Commutation is an assumed input for the exponential product formula, not a conclusion recovered from that formula; no converse exponential characterization is asserted.

For a finite parameter $\lambda\ge0$, the **Poisson count law**
$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$ is the probability measure on
$\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ whose masses are
$$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\{k\}=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!},\qquad k\in\mathbb N_0,$$
when $\lambda>0$, and is the point mass at $0$ when $\lambda=0$. The
normalization and the moment and generating-function identities used below are
proved in [[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]. The separate
extended convention for a Poisson point-process count on a Borel set of infinite
intensity is that the count equals $+\infty$ almost surely; it is not a finite
Poisson probability law.

$$q_{ij}\ge0\quad(i\ne j),\qquad \sum_{i<n}q_{ij}=0\quad(j<n).$$

has nonnegative entries and every column sums to one. If $\nu=0$, then $Q=0$.

For a finite parameter $\lambda\ge0$, the **Poisson count law**
$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$ is the probability measure on
$\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ whose masses are
$$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\{k\}=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!},\qquad k\in\mathbb N_0,$$
when $\lambda>0$, and is the point mass at $0$ when $\lambda=0$. The
normalization and the moment and generating-function identities used below are
proved in [[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]. The separate
extended convention for a Poisson point-process count on a Borel set of infinite
intensity is that the count equals $+\infty$ almost surely; it is not a finite
Poisson probability law.

For finite $\lambda\ge0$, the masses in
[[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]] sum to one. If $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$,
then
$$\mathbb E[N]=\lambda,\qquad \mathbb E[N(N-1)]=\lambda^2,\qquad \mathbb E[N^2]=\lambda^2+\lambda,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(N)=\lambda,$$
and $\mathbb E[s^N]=\exp(\lambda(s-1))$ for $0\le s\le1$.

For a finite real square matrix $A$, define

$$e^{tA}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^kA^k}{k!}.$$

This series converges absolutely and uniformly for $t$ in every bounded interval. It is differentiable with $\frac{d}{dt}e^{tA}=Ae^{tA}=e^{tA}A$ and $e^{0A}=I$. If finite square matrices $A$ and $B$ commute, then $e^Ae^B=e^{A+B}$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Each term $P^kp_0$ is a probability vector, and the displayed Poisson mixture is a probability vector. If $\nu=0$, then $Q=0$ and $p(t)=p_0$.

$$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\{k\}=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!},\qquad k\in\mathbb N_0,$$
when $\lambda>0$, and is the point mass at $0$ when $\lambda=0$. The

For $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\mu)$ with $\mu\ge0$ and integer $K\ge0$, write $\tau_K(\mu):=\mathbb P(N>K)$. If $\mu=0$, then $\tau_K(\mu)=0$. If $\mu>0$ and $\mu<K+2$, then

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be the function space of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], with $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$.

### The $p$-norm, for a rational exponent $p \ge 1$

Let $p \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $p \ge 1$. For $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_p \;:=\; \Bigl(\sum_{k<n} |x_k|^{p}\Bigr)^{1/p},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]), the sum is the finite
sum of [[def-finite-sum]], and both powers are the **rational** powers of
[[def-rational-power]].

**Every power written here is defined.** Each base $|x_k|$ is a nonnegative real
and $p > 0$, so $|x_k|^{p}$ is given by [[def-rational-power]] for $|x_k| > 0$
and by its supplementary clause $0^{p} = 0$ for $|x_k| = 0$; the sum of these
nonnegative terms is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), and
$1/p$ is a positive rational, so the outer power is defined for the same two
reasons. The value does not depend on which representative of $p$ or of $1/p$ is
used ([[lem-rational-power-well-defined]]).

**The exponent is rational in this definition.**
[[def-rational-power]] supplies the nonnegative-base powers used here, and
[[thm-minkowski-finite]] supplies the corresponding triangle inequality for
rational $p \ge 1$. This item makes no claim with $p$ ranging over a real
interval; its rational domain is unchanged.

### The maximum norm

For $n \ge 1$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_\infty \;:=\; \max\{\, |x_k| \;:\; k < n \,\},$$

the maximum of a nonempty finite set of reals, which exists and is one of its
elements ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is required and propagates.** At $n = 0$ the set
$\{|x_k| : k<n\}$ is empty and has no maximum ([[def-max-min]]). This is the same
restriction the published [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] carries, for the same reason, and
**every statement on this page that mentions $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$ inherits
it**. The $p$-norms for rational $p \ge 1$ carry no such restriction: at $n = 0$
each is the empty sum raised to a positive rational power, hence $0$.

### The three cases the rest of the page uses

- $\lVert x\rVert_1 = \sum_{k<n}|x_k|$, since $t^{1} = t$ for $t \ge 0$
  ([[lem-rational-power-laws]], and $0^{1} = 0$ by the supplementary clause).
- $\lVert x\rVert_2 = \bigl(\sum_{k<n}|x_k|^{2}\bigr)^{1/2} = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}x_k^{2}}$,
  which is exactly the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: the
  exponent $2$ agrees with the integer power, so $|x_k|^{2} = x_k^{2}$
  ([[lem-of-abs-value]]), and $t^{1/2}$ is the unique nonnegative square root of
  $t$, which is $\sqrt{t}$ ([[def-rational-power]], [[thm-of-square-roots]]).
  **The two notations denote the same function and no second Euclidean norm is
  introduced.**
- $\lVert x\rVert_\infty$ as above, for $n \ge 1$.

That each of these is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]], and
that the metrics they induce are exactly the published $d_1$, $d_2$ and
$d_\infty$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], is
[[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]; it is proved there
and is not assumed here.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

**The value is a finite nonnegative real.** For $n\ge 1$ the norms
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

**At $n=0$ the convention is explicit.** The only element of $\mathbb{R}^{0}$
is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

The induced quantity is a norm on the matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$:
for each rational $p\ge1$, and likewise for the separately named
$\infty$-case when $m,n\ge1$, separation, absolute homogeneity and the triangle
inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ with $m\ge 1$ and $n\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$, with the induced $1$-norm and the
separately defined induced $\infty$-norm of
[[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

1. **Maximum column sum.** $\lVert A\rVert_1=\max_{j<n}\sum_{i<m}|a_{ij}|$.
2. **Maximum row sum.** $\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|$.

Let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$ and let $m,n,q\in\mathbb{N}$, with the
induced $p$-norms of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

1. **Compatibility.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and every
   $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert Ax\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert x\rVert_p.$$
2. **Submultiplicativity.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and
   $B\in M_{n\times q}(\mathbb{R})$,
   $$\lVert AB\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert B\rVert_p.$$
3. **Normalisation.** For every $n\ge 1$,
   $$\lVert I_n\rVert_p=1,$$
   where $I_n$ is the identity matrix of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]];

**Inputs.** A finite column generator $Q$, a column probability vector $p_0$, $t\ge0$, an admissible rate $\nu\ge\max_jr_j$, a positive tail budget $\varepsilon$, a positive integer total-term cap $B$, and either exact real arithmetic or a validated arithmetic backend. In a rounded execution, the backend must certify the scalar control decisions defining $m$ and $\mu$, each finite tail-budget comparison, and an outward upper bound $T\ge mG_K(\mu)$; it must also return a certified $\ell^1$ error bound $E_{\rm alg}:=\|\widehat p-R_{\mu,K}^mp_0\|_1$ for its computed vector. The vector bound includes any arithmetic error from the weights, time split, and matrix-free $P$ actions. If any scalar or vector certificate is unavailable, return `certificate-unavailable`.

**Outputs.** Return $(p_0,0,0)$ when $\nu=0$ or $t=0$. Otherwise return `budget-exhausted` or `certificate-unavailable`, or an approximate vector $\widehat p$ and certified bounds $(T,E_{\rm alg})$ for which $\|p(t)-\widehat p\|_1\le T+E_{\rm alg}$. Here $T\ge mG_K(\mu)$ is an outward-certified Poisson-tail upper bound and $E_{\rm alg}$ bounds the arithmetic/algebraic error relative to the exact truncated accumulation. In exact real arithmetic, $T=mG_K(\mu)$ and $E_{\rm alg}=0$.

**Procedure.** For $\nu t>0$, set $m=\lceil\nu t\rceil$ and $\mu=\nu t/m$, so $0<\mu\le1$. A rounded backend must certify these values and inequalities; if it cannot, return `certificate-unavailable`. If $m>B$, return `budget-exhausted`. Set $K_{\max}=\lfloor B/m\rfloor-1$. Search the finite list $K=0,1,\ldots,K_{\max}$ for a member satisfying

$$G_K(\mu):=\frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^{K+1}}{(K+1)!\left(1-\mu/(K+2)\right)}\le\varepsilon/m.$$

In rounded arithmetic, accept a candidate only when a validated upper enclosure proves the displayed inequality, and set $T$ to a validated upper bound for $mG_K(\mu)$. If no candidate works, return `budget-exhausted` when the comparisons certify that every candidate fails, and `certificate-unavailable` when they do not decide the search. In exact arithmetic set $T=mG_K(\mu)$. Set $P=I+Q/\nu$ and $x_0=p_0$. For each substep $j=1,\ldots,m$, initialize $v_0=x_{j-1}$, $w_0=e^{-\mu}$, and $x_j=w_0v_0$. For $k=0,\ldots,K-1$, update

$$v_{k+1}=Pv_k,\qquad w_{k+1}=w_k\frac{\mu}{k+1},\qquad x_j\leftarrow x_j+w_{k+1}v_{k+1}.$$

These $P$ actions use the exact operator-application interface of [[def-matrix-free-access-model-for-krylov-methods]]: the routine supplies $v\mapsto Pv$ and vector additions and scalar multiples, without requiring stored matrix entries. No CSR representation, operation-count estimate, or convergence claim is part of this procedure. The exact term count is $m(K+1)\le B$ and the certified tail bound satisfies $T\le\varepsilon$. Never replace a tail certificate by floating-point $1-\sum_{k\le K}w_k$.

For a finite real square matrix $A$, define

$$e^{tA}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^kA^k}{k!}.$$

This series converges absolutely and uniformly for $t$ in every bounded interval. It is differentiable with $\frac{d}{dt}e^{tA}=Ae^{tA}=e^{tA}A$ and $e^{0A}=I$. If finite square matrices $A$ and $B$ commute, then $e^Ae^B=e^{A+B}$.

derivations.claim: For any $\mu>0$, set $S_\mu=e^{\mu Q/\nu}=e^{-\mu}e^{\mu P}$ and $R_{\mu,K}=\sum_{k=0}^K w_k(\mu)P^k$. By [F1], each $P^k$ is nonnegative and column stochastic; [F2] and [F3] give $S_\mu=\sum_{k\ge0}w_k(\mu)P^k$ with nonnegative weights summing to one. Thus $R_{\mu,K}$ is nonnegative with common column sum $s_K:=\sum_{k=0}^K w_k(\mu)\le1$, and $S_\mu-R_{\mu,K}$ is nonnegative with common column sum $\tau_K(\mu)$.

The induced norm formula [F6] gives $\|S_\mu\|_1=1$, $\|R_{\mu,K}\|_1=s_K$, and $\|S_\mu-R_{\mu,K}\|_1=\tau_K(\mu)$. If $\lambda=\nu t=0$, only the $k=0$ Poisson weight is nonzero, so $p(t)=u_K(t)=p_0$ and the omitted mass is zero. If $\lambda>0$, apply step 1.1 with $\mu=\lambda$: $(S_\lambda-R_{\lambda,K})p_0$ is nonnegative and its coordinate sum is $\tau_K(\lambda)$; by [F5], the exact one-series $\ell^1$ omitted mass is therefore exactly the scalar Poisson tail.

In the time-split algorithm, $0<\mu\le1$ and $K\ge0$, so $\mu<K+2$ and [F4] gives $\tau_K(\mu)\le G_K(\mu)$. For $m$ substeps the telescoping identity $S_\mu^m-R_{\mu,K}^m=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}S_\mu^{m-1-j}(S_\mu-R_{\mu,K})R_{\mu,K}^j$, [F5]–[F6], and step 2.1 give $\|S_\mu^m-R_{\mu,K}^m\|_1\le m\tau_K(\mu)\le mG_K(\mu)$.

Every term in the telescoping identity is nonnegative, so the exact vector error on $p_0$ is nonnegative. Each column sum of $S_\mu^m$ is one and each column sum of $R_{\mu,K}^m$ is $s_K^m$; hence its $\ell^1$ mass is exactly $1-s_K^m=1-(1-\tau_K(\mu))^m\le m\tau_K(\mu)$. This proves the exact time-split lost-mass identity and the preceding error bound.

Since $m\mu=\nu t$, [F8] gives $S_\mu^m=e^{tQ}$ and [F2] gives $S_\mu^mp_0=p(t)$, while [F7] identifies the exact truncated output as $R_{\mu,K}^mp_0$. The triangle inequality for the vector $1$-norm [F5] therefore yields $\|p(t)-\widehat u\|_1\le\|p(t)-R_{\mu,K}^mp_0\|_1+\|R_{\mu,K}^mp_0-\widehat u\|_1\le mG_K(\mu)+E_{\rm alg}\le T+E_{\rm alg}$ when the validated upper bound $T$ is supplied. If $\nu t=0$, the algorithm returns $p_0$ and both error terms are zero.

Let $S$ be a nonempty at most countable state space, and let $q(x,y)\ge0$ be a finite transition rate for each pair $x,y\in S$ with $x\ne y$. Require the total exit rate

$$\lambda(x):=\sum_{y\ne x}q(x,y)$$

to be finite for every $x$. The associated **column rate matrix convention** is $Q_{yx}=q(x,y)$ for $y\ne x$ and $Q_{xx}=-\lambda(x)$; thus the source state indexes the column. No finite-dimensional matrix is asserted for an infinite $S$.

A **given time-homogeneous pure-jump Markov chain with rates $q$** is a process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ with values in $S$ whose conditional future law given its history depends only on its present state and elapsed time, and whose paths are constant between successive jumps. Its transition kernels $K_t$ depend only on elapsed time, satisfy $K_0=I$, and obey $K_{s+t}=K_sK_t$ using the composition $(K_sK_t)(x,A):=\int_S K_t(z,A)\,K_s(x,dz)$ of [[def-composition-of-probability-kernels]]. At state $x$ with $\lambda(x)>0$, its holding time has survival $e^{-\lambda(x)t}$ and its next state is $y\ne x$ with probability $q(x,y)/\lambda(x)$, independently of that holding time; at $\lambda(x)=0$ it stays at $x$. It is **nonexplosive** when almost surely it has only finitely many state changes on every bounded time interval.

The chain and nonexplosion are input hypotheses in this item and in the projection results below. This definition does not construct a chain from an arbitrary countable rate matrix and proves no general nonexplosion claim.

Let $X$ be a given nonexplosive chain as in [[def-xd-countable-nonexplosive-ctmc]], with initial law $p_0$ on $S$, and let $F\subseteq S$ be finite and nonempty. Its first exit time from $F$ is

$$\tau_F:=\inf\{s\ge0:X_s\notin F\},$$

with $\tau_F=0$ when $X_0\notin F$. Adjoin a new state $\dagger\notin S$ and define the **killed projection** $Y_t=X_t$ for $t<\tau_F$ and $Y_t=\dagger$ for $t\ge\tau_F$. The **killed mass vector** is $u_F(t,x):=\mathbb P(Y_t=x)$ for $x\in F$, and the **cemetery mass** is $c_F(t):=\mathbb P(Y_t=\dagger)$. Initially, $u_F(0,x)=p_0(x)$ for $x\in F$ and $c_F(0)=p_0(S\setminus F)$.

For $x\in F$ let $\lambda(x)=\sum_{y\ne x}q(x,y)$. The killed principal subgenerator on $F$ has entries $(Q_F)_{y x}=q(x,y)$ for $y\ne x$ in $F$ and $(Q_F)_{x x}=-\lambda(x)$; its column sum is $-\sum_{y\notin F}q(x,y)$. The **cemetery lift** is the finite matrix $\widetilde Q_F$ on $F\cup\{\dagger\}$ with these same entries on $F$, with

$$\widetilde Q_{\dagger x}=\lambda(x)-\sum_{\substack{y\in F\\y\ne x}}q(x,y)=\sum_{y\notin F}q(x,y)\quad(x\in F),\qquad \widetilde Q_{x\dagger}=0\quad(x\in F),\qquad \widetilde Q_{\dagger\dagger}=0.$$

Every column of $\widetilde Q_F$ sums to zero and its off-diagonal entries are nonnegative, so it is a finite column generator in the sense of [[def-xd-finite-column-generator]]. The cemetery state is absorbing; trajectories that return to $F$ after their first exit remain at $\dagger$ in this projection.

Let $Q$ be an $n\times n$ finite column generator, let $p_0$ be a column probability vector, and let $t\ge0$. The unique differentiable solution of

$$p'(t)=Qp(t),\qquad p(0)=p_0,$$

is $p(t)=e^{tQ}p_0$. If $\nu>0$ and $\nu\ge\max_jr_j$, put $P=I+Q/\nu$; then

$$p(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}e^{-\nu t}\frac{(\nu t)^k}{k!}P^kp_0.$$

Each term $P^kp_0$ is a probability vector, and the displayed Poisson mixture is a probability vector. If $\nu=0$, then $Q=0$ and $p(t)=p_0$.

Let $S$ be at most countable. For nonnegative functions $a,b:S\to[0,\infty)$ with finite total masses, define

$$\|a-b\|_{\ell^1(S)}:=\sum_{x\in S}|a(x)-b(x)|.$$

For a nonnegative family, $\sum_{x\in S}$ means the supremum of its finite subsums; this agrees with the ordinary series under any enumeration of $S$. The distance is finite because $|a(x)-b(x)|\le a(x)+b(x)$ termwise, so $\|a-b\|_{\ell^1(S)}\le\sum_xa(x)+\sum_xb(x)$. In particular it is defined for probability and subprobability mass functions.

For every real $x$,
$$1+x\le\exp(x).$$
Consequently, if $0\le p\le1$ and $m\in\mathbb N$, then
$$ (1-p)^m\le\exp(-mp). $$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
For every real $x$, the series $\sum_{n\ge0}x^n/\iota(n!)$ converges absolutely. Its power-series radius is therefore $+\infty$.

derivations.claim: For each source state $x\in F$, the off-diagonal entries of $\widetilde Q_F$ are the internal rates $q(x,y)$ and the exit rate to $\dagger$ is $\sum_{y\notin F}q(x,y)$. Their sum is $\lambda(x)$, so the diagonal $-\lambda(x)$ makes the column sum zero. The cemetery column is zero. Therefore $\widetilde Q_F$ is a finite column generator.

By the definition of $Y$, for each $x\in F$ the event $\{Y_t=x\}$ is exactly $\{X_t=x,\tau_F>t\}$; the complementary event $\{Y_t=\dagger\}$ is $\{\tau_F\le t\}$. Therefore $u_F(t,x)=\mathbb P(X_t=x,\tau_F>t)\le p_t(x)$ and $c_F(t)=\mathbb P(\tau_F\le t)$. Returning paths are included in $p_t$ but excluded from $u_F$ by the strict first-exit condition.

Let $M_F=\max_{x\in F}\lambda(x)$, finite because $F$ is finite. For $0\le h\le1$, [F6] bounds the exponential series remainder by $|e^{-\lambda(x)h}-(1-\lambda(x)h)|\le h^2\sum_{k\ge2}\lambda(x)^k/k!$, so no-jump probability is $1-\lambda(x)h+o(h)$ uniformly on finite $F$. If $\lambda(x)>0$, the first-jump probability $1-e^{-\lambda(x)h}=\lambda(x)h+o(h)$ multiplied by the destination probability $q(x,y)/\lambda(x)$ from [F1] gives rate $q(x,y)h+o(h)$ for each $y\ne x$; if $\lambda(x)=0$, all rates from $x$ are zero and these probabilities are zero. For the aggregate exit event, its conditional destination probability is $a_x/\lambda(x)$ when $\lambda(x)>0$, so its probability is $a_xh+o(h)$; when $\lambda(x)=0$, $a_x=0$ and this probability is zero. Here $a_x=\lambda(x)-\sum_{y\in F,y\ne x}q(x,y)\ge0$. After reaching $\dagger$ there are no further changes. By [F5] applied to $-u$, $1-e^{-u}\le u$ for $u\ge0$, so the probability of a first change within $h$ is at most $M_Fh$; conditional on a first change that stays in $F$, a second change within the remaining time has probability at most $M_Fh$. Hence the probability of two or more changes is at most $M_F^2h^2$. Thus the finite transition matrix of $Y$ is $I+h\widetilde Q_F+o(h)$ as $h\downarrow0$, uniformly over its finite state space.

Extend $u_F$ by zero outside $F$. For $x\in F$, $p_t(x)-u_F(t,x)\ge0$ by step 1.2; for $x\notin F$, the difference is $p_t(x)\ge0$. Summing these nonnegative differences over $S$ gives $1-\sum_{x\in F}u_F(t,x)=1-\mathbb P(\tau_F>t)=c_F(t)$. By [F4], this sum is exactly $\|p_t-\bar u_F(t)\|_{\ell^1(S)}$.

The process $Y$ is Markov: before killing this follows from the Markov property of $X$, and after killing its state $\dagger$ is absorbing. Hence its finite column transition matrix $T_Y(h)$ satisfies $T_Y(h)=I+h\widetilde Q_F+o(h)$ entrywise by step 2.1, and its law satisfies $\widetilde p(t+h)=T_Y(h)\widetilde p(t)$. This gives the right derivative $\widetilde Q_F\widetilde p(t)$. For $t>0$, $\widetilde p(t)=T_Y(h)\widetilde p(t-h)$. Since the state space has finitely many coordinates, the entrywise expansion and $\sum_j\widetilde p_j(t-h)=1$ imply each coordinate of $\widetilde p(t)-\widetilde p(t-h)$ is $O(h)$; hence $\widetilde p(t-h)\to\widetilde p(t)$. Dividing the identity by $h$ and using the entrywise limit $(T_Y(h)-I)/h\to\widetilde Q_F$ gives the left derivative $\widetilde Q_F\widetilde p(t)$ as well, because every coordinate is a finite sum. Thus $\widetilde p'=\widetilde Q_F\widetilde p$ with initial law $\widetilde p(0)$. By [F3], $\widetilde p(t)=e^{t\widetilde Q_F}\widetilde p(0)$.

Let $a=\inf f$, $b=\sup f$, and $c=(a+b)/2=f(\dagger)$. The coupling uses the same path $X$: on $\{\tau_F>t\}$, $Y_t=X_t$, and on $\{\tau_F\le t\}$, $Y_t=\dagger$. Thus $|\mathbb E f(X_t)-\mathbb E f(Y_t)|=|\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{\tau_F\le t\}}(f(X_t)-c)]|\le\tfrac12(b-a)\mathbb P(\tau_F\le t)=\tfrac12\operatorname{osc}(f)c_F(t)$, as asserted.

**Inputs.** A given nonexplosive chain $X$ and initial law $p_0$; a finite positive integer $N$ and an explicitly supplied nested list of nonempty finite sets $F_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq F_N$; for each $F_i$, its exact finite cemetery-lift generator $\widetilde Q_{F_i}$ and lifted initial vector from [[def-xd-finite-state-projection-and-cemetery-lift]]; final time $T\ge0$; tolerance $\varepsilon>0$; a positive integer per-projection term cap $B$; and an arithmetic mode that is either exact real arithmetic or a validated arithmetic backend satisfying the requirements below and of [[alg-xd-budgeted-uniformization-accumulation]].

The supplied lift data must be the exact rates and initial masses of the given chain. An implementation may obtain the cemetery rate from the exact exit rate minus the finite sum of within-$F_i$ rates. A validated backend must certify the lift-rate calculation and its admissibility, the solver's scalar and vector certificates, and an outward enclosure of each computed cemetery coordinate, including the certified arithmetic/algebraic error required by [[thm-xd-uniformization-truncation-and-error]]; if any required certificate is unavailable, the corresponding projection is uncertified.

**Procedure.** For $i=1,\ldots,N$ in order:

1. Let $r_{i,z}:=-(\widetilde Q_{F_i})_{zz}$ for $z\in F_i\cup\{\dagger\}$ and set $\nu_i:=\max_{z\in F_i\cup\{\dagger\}}r_{i,z}=\max_{x\in F_i}\lambda(x)$; this includes the cemetery state's zero exit rate. If a validated backend cannot certify $\nu_i$ and its admissibility, treat the solver status as `certificate-unavailable`. Otherwise apply [[alg-xd-budgeted-uniformization-accumulation]] to $(\widetilde Q_{F_i},\widetilde p_{F_i,0},T)$ with admissible rate $\nu_i$, positive tail budget $\varepsilon$, term cap $B$, and the supplied arithmetic mode. If $\nu_i=0$, use the solver's zero-rate branch. If the status is `budget-exhausted` or `certificate-unavailable`, or the exact lift data are unavailable, return `inconclusive` with the statuses and all completed projection records; do not skip an uncertified projection.
2. Let $\widehat c_i$ be the computed cemetery coordinate. If the solver returns tail and arithmetic/algebraic error bounds $T_i$ and $E_{{\rm alg},i}$, put $\delta_i:=T_i+E_{{\rm alg},i}$, the total certified $\ell^1$ error bound. Form the outward-certified interval
   $$L_i=\max(0,\widehat c_i-\delta_i),\qquad U_i=\min(1,\widehat c_i+\delta_i).$$
   Record $F_i$, $\nu_i$, the computed vector, $\widehat c_i$, $[L_i,U_i]$, its tail bound $T_i$, and its arithmetic/algebraic error $E_{{\rm alg},i}$.
3. If exact comparison or validated interval arithmetic certifies $U_i\le\varepsilon$, return `certified` with this projection and its record.

If all $N$ projections have valid records but none passes the tolerance, return `inconclusive` with every record. The algorithm uses at most $N$ projections and $NB$ uniformization terms. It makes no claim that some finite projection outside this supplied list meets $\varepsilon$.

Let $X_t$ be a given nonexplosive countable chain with rates $q(x,y)$, initial law $p_0$, and finite exit rates as in [[def-xd-countable-nonexplosive-ctmc]]. For a finite nonempty $F\subseteq S$, let $\tau_F$ and $Y_t$ be the killed projection of [[def-xd-finite-state-projection-and-cemetery-lift]]. Write $p_t(x)=\mathbb P(X_t=x)$ and $u_F(t,x)=\mathbb P(Y_t=x)$ for $x\in F$. Then

$$u_F(t,x)=\mathbb P(X_t=x,\tau_F>t)\le p_t(x),\qquad c_F(t)=\mathbb P(\tau_F\le t).$$

If $\bar u_F$ is $u_F$ extended by zero to $S\setminus F$, then

$$\|p_t-\bar u_F(t)\|_{\ell^1(S)}=c_F(t).$$

For any bounded real observable $f:S\to\mathbb R$, put $\operatorname{osc}(f):=\sup_{x\in S}f(x)-\inf_{x\in S}f(x)$ and extend it to the cemetery state by $f(\dagger):=(\sup f+\inf f)/2$. The corresponding expectation error obeys

$$|\mathbb E[f(X_t)]-\mathbb E[f(Y_t)]|\le\tfrac12\operatorname{osc}(f)c_F(t).$$

The finite cemetery lift $\widetilde Q_F$ in [[def-xd-finite-state-projection-and-cemetery-lift]] is a finite generator and $\mathcal L(Y_t)=e^{t\widetilde Q_F}\mathcal L(Y_0)$. A path that exits $F$ and later returns contributes to the full marginal but remains at the cemetery state in the killed projection.

Let $Q$ be a finite column generator, $p_0$ a column probability vector, and $\nu>0$ an admissible rate. For $\lambda=\nu t$ and $K\ge0$, the exact one-series partial sum

$$u_K(t):=\sum_{k=0}^{K}e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}P^kp_0$$

is nonnegative and substochastic, and its exact $\ell^1$ distance from $p(t)$ is the scalar Poisson tail $\tau_K(\lambda)=\mathbb P(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)>K)$. If $\nu t>0$, the budgeted algorithm sets $m=\lceil\nu t\rceil$ and $\mu=\nu t/m\le1$, and uses $R_{\mu,K}=\sum_{k=0}^K e^{-\mu}\mu^kP^k/k!$. Then $R_{\mu,K}^m p_0$ is nonnegative and substochastic, and its exact transient $\ell^1$ error is

$$1-\left(\sum_{k=0}^{K}e^{-\mu}\frac{\mu^k}{k!}\right)^m\le m\tau_K(\mu)\le mG_K(\mu).$$

If a computed vector $\widehat u$ has a separately certified accumulated arithmetic/algebraic error $E_{\rm alg}:=\|\widehat u-R_{\mu,K}^mp_0\|_1$, then $\|p(t)-\widehat u\|_1\le mG_K(\mu)+E_{\rm alg}$. In rounded arithmetic, if $T$ is a validated upper bound for $mG_K(\mu)$, then $\|p(t)-\widehat u\|_1\le T+E_{\rm alg}$. The geometric tail certificate is not obtained by floating-point subtraction from one.

It either returns during one of these calls or after the last candidate, so it terminates after at most $N$ projections and $NB$ terms.

Suppose the algorithm returns `certified` at index $i$. By [F3], $|\widehat c_i-c_{F_i}(T)|\le\delta_i$. Since $0\le c_{F_i}(T)\le1$, the interval endpoints in [F1] enclose $c_{F_i}(T)$; hence $c_{F_i}(T)\le U_i\le\varepsilon$.

If no candidate passes, or a finite solver returns an unavailable certificate, [F1] specifies `inconclusive`; the procedure has examined only the supplied finite list and therefore establishes no existence claim for a projection outside that list.

Let $S=\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}$ with $n\ge1$. Identify its real matrices with $M_n(\mathbb R)$, the finite matrix space with row and column indices in $S$ from [[def-matrix-space]], and use the matrix-product and identity conventions of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. A **finite column generator** on $S$ is a real matrix $Q=(q_{ij})\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ satisfying

$$q_{ij}\ge0\quad(i\ne j),\qquad \sum_{i<n}q_{ij}=0\quad(j<n).$$

The column index $j$ is the source state and the row index $i$ is the destination state: for $i\ne j$, $q_{ij}$ is the transition rate from $j$ to $i$. The exit rate from $j$ is

$$r_j:=-q_{jj}=\sum_{i\ne j}q_{ij}\ge0.$$

A **column probability vector** is $p\in\mathbb R^n$ with $p_i\ge0$ for each $i$ and $\sum_{i<n}p_i=1$. A **subprobability vector** has the same coordinatewise nonnegativity and has coordinate sum at most one. These conventions are used throughout this page.

Let $Q$ be an $n\times n$ finite column generator, let $p_0$ be a column probability vector, and let $t\ge0$. The unique differentiable solution of

$$p'(t)=Qp(t),\qquad p(0)=p_0,$$

is $p(t)=e^{tQ}p_0$. If $\nu>0$ and $\nu\ge\max_jr_j$, put $P=I+Q/\nu$; then

$$p(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}e^{-\nu t}\frac{(\nu t)^k}{k!}P^kp_0.$$

Each term $P^kp_0$ is a probability vector, and the displayed Poisson mixture is a probability vector. If $\nu=0$, then $Q=0$ and $p(t)=p_0$.

For a finite parameter $\lambda\ge0$, the **Poisson count law**
$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$ is the probability measure on
$\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ whose masses are
$$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\{k\}=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!},\qquad k\in\mathbb N_0,$$
when $\lambda>0$, and is the point mass at $0$ when $\lambda=0$. The
normalization and the moment and generating-function identities used below are
proved in [[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]. The separate
extended convention for a Poisson point-process count on a Borel set of infinite
intensity is that the count equals $+\infty$ almost surely; it is not a finite
Poisson probability law.

For finite $\lambda\ge0$, the masses in
[[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]] sum to one. If $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$,
then
$$\mathbb E[N]=\lambda,\qquad \mathbb E[N(N-1)]=\lambda^2,\qquad \mathbb E[N^2]=\lambda^2+\lambda,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(N)=\lambda,$$
and $\mathbb E[s^N]=\exp(\lambda(s-1))$ for $0\le s\le1$.

Fix positive integers $d$ and $R$. A **reaction propensity system** consists of a state set $E\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ that is finite or countable, increments $\nu_j\in\mathbb Z^d$ for $1\le j\le R$, and propensities $a_j:E\to[0,\infty)$. Here “countable” means finite or countably infinite, as in [[def-countable]]. The total propensity
$$\lambda(x):=\sum_{j=1}^R a_j(x)$$
is finite for every $x\in E$, and $a_j(x)>0$ implies $x+\nu_j\in E$. Here $\mathbb N$ and $\mathbb Z$ have the meanings in [[def-natural-numbers]] and [[def-integers]], and addition in $\mathbb Z^d$ is coordinatewise.

A **reaction event** of channel $j$ at state $x$ records the marked transition $x\mapsto x+\nu_j$. The counting process $N_j(t)$ records the number of channel-$j$ events by time $t$. A zero increment $\nu_j=0$ is allowed: it records a reaction event without changing the state.

For a time-homogeneous system, the **reaction generator operator** on bounded functions $f:E\to\mathbb R$ is
$$(Qf)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(x)>0} a_j(x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr).$$
When $E$ is finite, $\Lambda:=\max_{x\in E}\lambda(x)<\infty$. If no active reaction has zero increment, the corresponding matrix has off-diagonal entries $q_{xy}=\sum_{j:x+\nu_j=y}a_j(x)$ and diagonal $q_{xx}=-\lambda(x)$. With zero-increment events, the operator formula remains valid and the matrix diagonal is instead minus the sum of state-changing rates; the zero-increment channels remain part of the marked event process.

For a finite horizon $T$, a **time-dependent propensity system** replaces $a_j(x)$ by functions $a_j:[0,T]\times E\to[0,\infty)$ whose sections $t\mapsto a_j(t,x)$ are measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B([0,T])$ of the usual topology on $[0,T]$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Require finite total rate $\lambda(t,x):=\sum_j a_j(t,x)$. Its time-dependent generator operator is
$$(Q_t f)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(t,x)>0} a_j(t,x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr).$$
This definition specifies a stochastic model. It does not assert that a physical chemical system follows that model.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $E\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ be countable and let a finite-channel system be as in [[def-reaction-network-propensity-system-and-generator]]. For an initial state $x_0\in E$, construct its minimal reaction process recursively: at state $x$, wait an exponential time with parameter $\lambda(x)$, choose channel $j$ with probability $a_j(x)/\lambda(x)$, and move to $x+\nu_j$; if $\lambda(x)=0$, remain at $x$ forever. Use an independent stream of these exponential and uniform random inputs, whose countable product law exists by Countable Choice and Dependent Choice.

For $V:E\to[1,\infty)$, call $V$ **proper** when $\{x:V(x)\le n\}$ is finite for every integer $n\ge1$. For this possibly unbounded $V$, define the finite local expression
$$(QV)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(x)>0}a_j(x)\bigl(V(x+\nu_j)-V(x)\bigr);$$
this does not assert that $V$ belongs to the bounded-function domain of the generator in [F1]. Suppose $QV\le cV$ for a constant $c\ge0$. Define $T_m$ as the time of the $m$th reaction event, with $T_m=\infty$ if fewer than $m$ events occur. Then the explosion time $\tau_\infty:=\lim_{m\to\infty}T_m$ satisfies $\mathbb P_{x_0}(\tau_\infty=\infty)=1$. No full Axiom of Choice is used.

Let $S$ be a nonempty at most countable state space, and let $q(x,y)\ge0$ be a finite transition rate for each pair $x,y\in S$ with $x\ne y$. Require the total exit rate

$$\lambda(x):=\sum_{y\ne x}q(x,y)$$

to be finite for every $x$. The associated **column rate matrix convention** is $Q_{yx}=q(x,y)$ for $y\ne x$ and $Q_{xx}=-\lambda(x)$; thus the source state indexes the column. No finite-dimensional matrix is asserted for an infinite $S$.

A **given time-homogeneous pure-jump Markov chain with rates $q$** is a process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ with values in $S$ whose conditional future law given its history depends only on its present state and elapsed time, and whose paths are constant between successive jumps. Its transition kernels $K_t$ depend only on elapsed time, satisfy $K_0=I$, and obey $K_{s+t}=K_sK_t$ using the composition $(K_sK_t)(x,A):=\int_S K_t(z,A)\,K_s(x,dz)$ of [[def-composition-of-probability-kernels]]. At state $x$ with $\lambda(x)>0$, its holding time has survival $e^{-\lambda(x)t}$ and its next state is $y\ne x$ with probability $q(x,y)/\lambda(x)$, independently of that holding time; at $\lambda(x)=0$ it stays at $x$. It is **nonexplosive** when almost surely it has only finitely many state changes on every bounded time interval.

The chain and nonexplosion are input hypotheses in this item and in the projection results below. This definition does not construct a chain from an arbitrary countable rate matrix and proves no general nonexplosion claim.

Let $X$ be a given nonexplosive chain as in [[def-xd-countable-nonexplosive-ctmc]], with initial law $p_0$ on $S$, and let $F\subseteq S$ be finite and nonempty. Its first exit time from $F$ is

$$\tau_F:=\inf\{s\ge0:X_s\notin F\},$$

with $\tau_F=0$ when $X_0\notin F$. Adjoin a new state $\dagger\notin S$ and define the **killed projection** $Y_t=X_t$ for $t<\tau_F$ and $Y_t=\dagger$ for $t\ge\tau_F$. The **killed mass vector** is $u_F(t,x):=\mathbb P(Y_t=x)$ for $x\in F$, and the **cemetery mass** is $c_F(t):=\mathbb P(Y_t=\dagger)$. Initially, $u_F(0,x)=p_0(x)$ for $x\in F$ and $c_F(0)=p_0(S\setminus F)$.

For $x\in F$ let $\lambda(x)=\sum_{y\ne x}q(x,y)$. The killed principal subgenerator on $F$ has entries $(Q_F)_{y x}=q(x,y)$ for $y\ne x$ in $F$ and $(Q_F)_{x x}=-\lambda(x)$; its column sum is $-\sum_{y\notin F}q(x,y)$. The **cemetery lift** is the finite matrix $\widetilde Q_F$ on $F\cup\{\dagger\}$ with these same entries on $F$, with

$$\widetilde Q_{\dagger x}=\lambda(x)-\sum_{\substack{y\in F\\y\ne x}}q(x,y)=\sum_{y\notin F}q(x,y)\quad(x\in F),\qquad \widetilde Q_{x\dagger}=0\quad(x\in F),\qquad \widetilde Q_{\dagger\dagger}=0.$$

Every column of $\widetilde Q_F$ sums to zero and its off-diagonal entries are nonnegative, so it is a finite column generator in the sense of [[def-xd-finite-column-generator]]. The cemetery state is absorbing; trajectories that return to $F$ after their first exit remain at $\dagger$ in this projection.

Let $Q$ be an $n\times n$ finite column generator, let $p_0$ be a column probability vector, and let $t\ge0$. The unique differentiable solution of

$$p'(t)=Qp(t),\qquad p(0)=p_0,$$

is $p(t)=e^{tQ}p_0$. If $\nu>0$ and $\nu\ge\max_jr_j$, put $P=I+Q/\nu$; then

$$p(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}e^{-\nu t}\frac{(\nu t)^k}{k!}P^kp_0.$$

Each term $P^kp_0$ is a probability vector, and the displayed Poisson mixture is a probability vector. If $\nu=0$, then $Q=0$ and $p(t)=p_0$.

Let $X_t$ be a given nonexplosive countable chain with rates $q(x,y)$, initial law $p_0$, and finite exit rates as in [[def-xd-countable-nonexplosive-ctmc]]. For a finite nonempty $F\subseteq S$, let $\tau_F$ and $Y_t$ be the killed projection of [[def-xd-finite-state-projection-and-cemetery-lift]]. Write $p_t(x)=\mathbb P(X_t=x)$ and $u_F(t,x)=\mathbb P(Y_t=x)$ for $x\in F$. Then

$$u_F(t,x)=\mathbb P(X_t=x,\tau_F>t)\le p_t(x),\qquad c_F(t)=\mathbb P(\tau_F\le t).$$

If $\bar u_F$ is $u_F$ extended by zero to $S\setminus F$, then

$$\|p_t-\bar u_F(t)\|_{\ell^1(S)}=c_F(t).$$

For any bounded real observable $f:S\to\mathbb R$, put $\operatorname{osc}(f):=\sup_{x\in S}f(x)-\inf_{x\in S}f(x)$ and extend it to the cemetery state by $f(\dagger):=(\sup f+\inf f)/2$. The corresponding expectation error obeys

$$|\mathbb E[f(X_t)]-\mathbb E[f(Y_t)]|\le\tfrac12\operatorname{osc}(f)c_F(t).$$

The finite cemetery lift $\widetilde Q_F$ in [[def-xd-finite-state-projection-and-cemetery-lift]] is a finite generator and $\mathcal L(Y_t)=e^{t\widetilde Q_F}\mathcal L(Y_0)$. A path that exits $F$ and later returns contributes to the full marginal but remains at the cemetery state in the killed projection.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: The system has two channels, increments $+1$ and $-1$, and propensities $a_+(n)=1$ and $a_-(n)=n$; the death channel is inactive at $n=0$, so every positive-propensity poststate remains in $\mathbb N_0$ and the total rate $1+n$ is finite. Thus [F1] applies.

Let $V(n)=1+n$. Its sublevel set $\{n:V(n)\le m\}$ is finite for each integer $m\ge1$, so $V$ is proper. For $n\ge1$, $QV(n)=1(V(n+1)-V(n))+n(V(n-1)-V(n))=1-n\le1+n=V(n)$; at $n=0$ the same value $QV(0)=1$ satisfies this bound. Hence [F2] with $c=1$ and [A1] proves the immigration-death chain is nonexplosive, as required by [F3].

On $F=\{0,1\}$, state $0$ jumps to $1$ at rate $1$; state $1$ jumps to $0$ at rate $1$ and exits to $2\notin F$ at rate $1$. These off-diagonal rates are nonnegative, and the cemetery construction [F4] gives the displayed $\widetilde Q_F$ with zero column sums. Multiplying by the lifted probability vector gives $p_0'=-p_0+p_1$, $p_1'=p_0-2p_1$, and $c_F'=p_1$, with initial vector $(1,0,0)^T$.

From $p_1'=p_0-2p_1$ we have $p_0=p_1'+2p_1$; differentiating and using $p_0'=-p_0+p_1$ yields $p_1''+3p_1'+p_1=0$, with $p_1(0)=0$ and $p_1'(0)=1$. The characteristic roots are $r_\pm=(-3\pm\sqrt5)/2$ and $r_+-r_-=\sqrt5$, so the unique solution is $p_1(t)=(e^{r_+t}-e^{r_-t})/\sqrt5$.

Since $c_F'=p_1$ and $c_F(0)=0$, integrating the expression in step 2.1 gives the displayed formula for $c_F(t)$. By [F6], this coordinate is $\mathbb P(\tau_F\le t)$ and equals the embedded killed-vector $\ell^1$ error.

Fix $t>0$ and choose ordered times $0<s_1<s_2<s_3<t$. The joint density for jumps $0\to1$ at $s_1$, $1\to2$ at $s_2$, and $2\to1$ at $s_3$, followed by no further jump through $t$, is $e^{-s_1}\cdot1\cdot e^{-2(s_2-s_1)}\cdot1\cdot e^{-3(s_3-s_2)}\cdot2\cdot e^{-2(t-s_3)}$, which is strictly positive; integrating this positive density over the nonempty ordered-time simplex gives positive probability. Let $S=\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}$ with $n\ge1$. Identify its real matrices with $M_n(\mathbb R)$, the finite matrix space with row and column indices in $S$ from [[def-matrix-space]], and use the matrix-product and identity conventions of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. A **finite column generator** on $S$ is a real matrix $Q=(q_{ij})\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ satisfying

$$q_{ij}\ge0\quad(i\ne j),\qquad \sum_{i<n}q_{ij}=0\quad(j<n).$$

The column index $j$ is the source state and the row index $i$ is the destination state: for $i\ne j$, $q_{ij}$ is the transition rate from $j$ to $i$. The exit rate from $j$ is

$$r_j:=-q_{jj}=\sum_{i\ne j}q_{ij}\ge0.$$

A **column probability vector** is $p\in\mathbb R^n$ with $p_i\ge0$ for each $i$ and $\sum_{i<n}p_i=1$. A **subprobability vector** has the same coordinatewise nonnegativity and has coordinate sum at most one. These conventions are used throughout this page.

Let $Q$ be an $n\times n$ finite column generator, let $p_0$ be a column probability vector, and let $t\ge0$. The unique differentiable solution of

$$p'(t)=Qp(t),\qquad p(0)=p_0,$$

is $p(t)=e^{tQ}p_0$. If $\nu>0$ and $\nu\ge\max_jr_j$, put $P=I+Q/\nu$; then

$$p(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}e^{-\nu t}\frac{(\nu t)^k}{k!}P^kp_0.$$

Each term $P^kp_0$ is a probability vector, and the displayed Poisson mixture is a probability vector. If $\nu=0$, then $Q=0$ and $p(t)=p_0$.

derivations.claim: $Q_A=0$ is a finite column generator, and the constant vector $p_A(t)=e_1$ solves $p_A'=Q_Ap_A$ with the stated initial value. By [F2] it is the unique law, and its mean is $0\cdot0+1\cdot1+2\cdot0=1$.

The off-diagonal entries of $Q_B$ are nonnegative and its columns sum to zero, so [F1] applies. Writing $p_B=(p_0,p_1,p_2)^T$, its master equation is $p_0'=p_1$, $p_1'=-2p_1$, $p_2'=p_1$ with initial values $(0,1,0)$. Solving gives $p_1=e^{-2t}$ and $p_0=p_2=(1-e^{-2t})/2$; direct differentiation verifies these formulas and their initial data, and [F2] makes this the unique law.

The mean under $p_B(t)$ is $0\cdot p_0+1\cdot p_1+2\cdot p_2=e^{-2t}+1-e^{-2t}=1$, the same as the mean under $p_A(t)$, while $p_B$ has positive mass at $0$ for $t>0$ and $p_A$ has none. Thus the same mean trajectory corresponds to two different full distributions.
